summary: Describes an RFC 3933 experiment to let the IETF community try a broader set of tools for managing mailing lists, such as long-term suspensions, beyond those in RFCs 3683 and 3934. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A club tries out new rules for dealing with people who disrupt group chats, to see if they work.

questions: how long can the iesg suspend posting rights
subtitle: A time-limited IETF process experiment that lets the IESG try mailing list sanctions between a 30-day suspension and a year-long ban.

tldr.problem: IETF rules left a large gap between the sanctions available for disruptive behavior on mailing lists: a 30-day suspension on one side, and an indefinite ban that can spread to every IETF list on the other.
tldr.mechanism: For 18 months the IESG may approve other methods of mailing list control, including suspensions longer than 30 days, on a specified set of lists, after announcing them publicly at least 14 days ahead.
tldr.outcome: It is an RFC 3933 experiment meant to gather input on long-term guidelines, and the RFC says it is not expected to become a permanent Best Current Practice in its current form. It has since been updated by RFC 8717.

today: RFC 4633 is an Experimental document and has been updated by RFC 8717. The RFC itself says the experiment was not expected to be adopted in its current form as a permanent Best Current Practice.

sections.title: The Gap in Mailing List Rules
sections.content:
As RFC 3683 explains, the IETF needs rules of conduct to limit disruptive or abusive behavior while keeping a fair and open forum. Over time several different rules piled up.

  • RFC 2418 let an Area Director, with IESG approval, ask a list maintainer to block an individual from posting, but only on working group lists.
  • The IETF discussion list charter (RFC 3005) lets the IETF Chair, the IETF Executive Director or a sergeant-at-arms restrict posting on ietf@ietf.org.
  • RFC 3683 bans named individuals from posting for at least one year, but once a ban exists for one list, the people running other IETF lists can unilaterally remove that individual's posting rights.
  • RFC 3934 lets a working group chair suspend a member's posting rights for 30 days, and appears to remove the earlier ability to approve longer suspensions.

The result, in the RFC's words, is a large gap between the levels of sanction that can be applied.
sections.eli5: There was a short time-out and a giant ban, and nothing in the middle.

sections.title: What Counts as an IETF Mailing List
sections.content: The experiment covers all IETF mailing lists, not only working group lists. The RFC defines an IETF mailing list as the IETF list itself, any list operated to further the work of a current working group, any list created for a working group but kept for discussion after it was shut down, any list created in support of an IETF-specified procedure (including lists for discussing registration actions), and any list hosted on a site or system operated by the IASA or otherwise on behalf of the IETF.
sections.eli5: It is about every official IETF group chat, not only the ones for working groups.

sections.title: The Experiment and Its Limits
sections.content:
The experiment runs for 18 months. During that time the IESG MAY approve other methods of mailing list control besides those in RFC 3683 and RFC 3934, for a specified set of lists. These include, but are not limited to, suspending an individual's posting rights beyond 30 days. The IESG may delegate the authority to carry out longer suspensions of specific individuals on specific lists.

Several limits apply. The procedures MUST NOT be used to suspend posting rights beyond the end of the experiment, and MUST NOT limit anyone's ability to read a list.

The IESG MUST publicly announce any approved procedure, including a description and the lists it covers (or that it covers all lists), at least 14 days before it takes effect. Community consensus is not required, although comments are encouraged. All active procedures MUST be published in an easy-to-find location, and sanctions can be appealed using the procedures in RFC 2026.
sections.eli5: For one and a half years the leaders can try new in-between punishments. They must warn everyone two weeks ahead, never stop people from reading, and the punishments end when the trial ends.

sections.title: How It Might Be Used
sections.content: This section is informative. The IESG could approve a procedure that lets it suspend someone from one or more lists for a fixed period longer than 30 days. It could also delegate that power in two ways. In the first, the IESG suspends a named individual from a list and gives that list's managers the delegated authority to keep applying longer suspensions if disruption continues. In the second, the IESG approves a procedure naming a set of lists and lets their managers act unilaterally after an initial suspension, in a manner similar to RFC 3683.
sections.eli5: The leaders could hand some of the power to the people running each chat, but only with the rules written down first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC describes a change to how the IETF manages mailing list discussions and states that it has no security considerations.
sections.eli5: This is a rule change about group chats, so there is no computer-security problem to worry about here.
